spine: Keep the useful role of reputation, expose when it substitutes for evidence, then examine incentives and claim-level institutions that make correction affordable.
art: An editorial inspection bench: deep plum and brass, translucent pedigree sleeves, separate evidence weights, reversible seals and claim cards with generous typographic hierarchy.
lines: Borrowed Credibility examines how scientific reputation can substitute for evidence without anyone intending deception.
The book begins from a necessary fact: nobody can independently verify everything they use.
Institutions therefore ration attention through names, affiliations, journals, and previous success.
The danger appears when those shortcuts acquire more authority than their evidence deserves.
Its constructive argument joins scientific incentives with ways to make verification cheaper and more specific.
Readers gain a framework for reforming trust without dismissing expertise or imagining universal corruption.
